statement: In how many ways can $105$ be written as the sum of two or more consecutive positive integers? (For example, $105 = 52 + 53$ is one way.)

choices.misconception: I only looked for lists with an odd number of terms, centered on a whole number, so I found $34 + 35 + 36$, $19 + \cdots + 23$ and $12 + \cdots + 18$.
I only looked for lists with an even number of terms, so I found only the lists with $2$, $6$, $10$ and $14$ terms.
I counted the $8$ odd divisors of $105$, but one of them corresponds to $105$ by itself, which is not a sum of two or more numbers.
I counted every divisor of $210$ except $1$ as a possible number of terms, without checking that the first term comes out a positive integer.

hints: If the sum has $k$ terms starting at $a$, then it equals $ka + \frac{k(k-1)}{2}$. Set this equal to $105$ and multiply by $2$.
$k(2a + k - 1) = 210$. The two factors $k$ and $2a + k - 1$ have opposite parity (their difference $2a - 1$ is odd), and $k$ is the smaller one.
Split $210$ into an even and an odd factor with the smaller one at least $2$. The odd part can be any of the odd divisors $1, 3, 5, 7, 15, 21, 35, 105$ of $105$.

solutions.reliable: A list of $k$ consecutive integers starting at $a$ has sum $ka + \frac{k(k-1)}{2}$, so we need $k(2a + k - 1) = 210$ with $k \ge 2$ and $a \ge 1$. The factors $k$ and $m = 2a + k - 1$ differ by $2a - 1$, an odd positive number, so one is odd, one is even, and $k < m$. Since $210 = 2 \cdot 105$, each odd divisor $o$ of $105$ gives exactly one factorization into an odd factor $o$ and an even factor $210 / o$, and $k$ is the smaller of the two. The odd divisors are $1, 3, 5, 7, 15, 21, 35, 105$, giving $k = 1, 3, 5, 7, 14, 10, 6, 2$. Throwing out $k = 1$ (just $105$ itself) leaves $7$ ways: $52 + 53$, $34 + \cdots + 36$, $19 + \cdots + 23$, $15 + \cdots + 20$, $12 + \cdots + 18$, $6 + \cdots + 15$ and $1 + \cdots + 14$.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
